# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why4: As strangers hear it, "a pair" never says a pair of what, so the step only makes sense if you already know it's glasses.

screens.instead: Order a pair of caption glasses, with free returns.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step (order a pair with free returns), asking whether to collect the people who'd take it is the obvious next move before the study goes out.
screens.why2: "Pilot" is everyday YC-founder language to me, and the hint spells out exactly what respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of deaf and hard-of-hearing people ready to try the glasses is entirely my own call.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and nothing is missing.
screens.why5: The respondent line, "Would you try this for real? Leave your email", is generic and drops the step I just typed (order a pair with 15-day free returns), so for hardware it reads more like a beta sign-up than my real ask.
screens.instead: Ask the people who say yes to leave their email so you can offer them a pair with free returns? (Yes, ask them / No, not yet)

screens.why1: Once I've picked how deaf and hard-of-hearing adults will answer, deciding who actually receives a link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: 'Who gets a link?' and the three routes are plain to me as a founder recruiting testers, and 'Contacts page' is Keel's own screen, which I've seen in the flow.
screens.why3: I know where my people are: users and waitlist names I can message one by one, plus HLAA chapters and deaf and hard-of-hearing groups online where an open link would go.
screens.why4: The three routes (named people, a Keel-found list, one open link in a group) are distinct and cover how I'd reach people, and I picked named people.
screens.why5: Nothing about AirCaps or my roles is changed here; it is purely about distribution and leaks nothing to a respondent.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it, 1 of 7 at 12 or more against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 1 for and 6 against plainly, but the unit 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' is garbled, and the marker at 5 sits on a 0-to-15 conversations axis while meaning 5 people, so I had to look twice to see where the bar is.
screens.why_b3: My Existing sacrifice was a money estimate of $200 to $1,500 a year spent on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras; turning it into 'about 12 conversations lost a month' is recognisable as the same pain, but it is not the belief I typed.
screens.why_b4: Pointing me to the Price card is a next step, but it does not say what a smaller loss than I estimated means for selling $599 glasses, for example whether to lead with the hardest situations like groups and noise.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says 7 people is a lean and not a call, but the headline 'they lose less today than you estimated' reads as a claim about all deaf and hard-of-hearing adults rather than these 7.
screens.instead: Not holding up, among these 7: only 1 of 7 missed 12 or more conversations last month (most missed 2 to 8), short of your bar of 5 of 7; a small group, so a lean. Consider leading with the group and noisy settings where the loss is worst, then check the Price card.

screens.why_b1: Not holding up sits right beside 0 of 7 at $599 or more, 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, and bar 5 of 7 on each, so I know the answer and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: Both charts show what is counted (up-front worth, then monthly worth) over 7 people, with my bar at 5 of 7 and my $599 and $20 marked as band low edges, though the two identical unlabelled strips take a beat to match to their charts.
screens.why_b3: Price at $599 up front then $20 a month is my site's ladder, not the $599 to $839 a year I checked, and it treats the $20 Pro plan as required when my glasses come with free unlimited captions, so a monthly answer under $20 counts against a price I don't actually charge everyone.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats that 6 of 7 sit at $250 to under $599 and sends me to the Insights tab, without saying whether to test a lower up-front price, lead with the free plan, or offer the try-before-you-buy pair three people asked for.
screens.why_b5: 7 answered and 7 counted is on screen, the small group is called a lean, not a call, and nothing claims more than the 7 answers show.
screens.instead: Not holding up: none of 7 would pay $599 up front, 6 of 7 put it at $250 to under $599; since captions are free and Pro is optional, the up-front price is the real gap, so test a price under $599 or a loaner pair before ordering.

screens.why_b1: The 'Not reached' verdict sits right beside its deciding number, '0 of 7 named your price or more', and the reason (nothing to ask) is tied to it.
screens.why_b2: An all-zero chart plainly counts where the money would come from, but the strip draws 5 ghost cells against 7 people who answered, so I need a second look to tell how many it is over and where my bar sits.
screens.why_b3: Ability to pay is a check Keel derived from my price and cost estimate, not a line I typed, though the $599 then $20 a month framing is recognisably mine.
screens.why_b4: The So line says this check waits on price until 5 name it, but it does not say what that means for me, such as that the price question has to be settled first or what the named ranges ($250 to under $599, mostly under $20 a month) suggest.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible and nothing is claimed beyond it, but 'only 0 of 7' is odd wording, the small sample is never called small, and the 5-cell strip against 7 people can mislead.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of 7 would pay $599 then $20 a month (six named $250 to under $599, all under $20 a month), so nobody was asked where the money would come from. Settle price first; the answers point nearer $499 and $10 a month.

screens.why_b1: The card says 'Holding up' with '6 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7' right under it, so I know the belief held and by how much it cleared the bar.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers to who had to agree across 7 people: 6 for, 1 against. The strip marks my bar at 5, so I see at once that 6 clears it.
screens.why_b3: 'Buyer and payer' and 'The deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else has to agree' are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count. It doesn't tell me what to do: the wearer is the right person to sell to, so the blocker on the money page is price and spend, not who signs off.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so the holding verdict isn't oversold, even though the So line's 'They decide alone' reads a little flat.
screens.instead: Holding up, as a lean on 7 people: the wearer decides alone, so sell straight to them (HSA/FSA helps). The money stage fails on price and on what they spend today, not on who has to agree.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, '6 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7', and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts answers to the order question over 7 people, with the marker at 5 and the strip showing 6 for and 1 against, so all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card's title and belief line are exactly what I checked: 'Commitment' and 'Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order a pair with free returns now.'
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is a concrete action, but it ignores that the same seven put 0 of 7 at $599 on the Price card, so this yes means 'try it with free returns' and not 'buy it'.
screens.why_b5: The count line correctly says 'a lean, not a call', but the So line's flat 'Book them into it' treats a hypothetical, risk-free yes from 7 people as a firm order.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 would try a pair with free returns, but none valued it at $599 (Price card): offer them the trial and watch how many keep the glasses past 15 days. Seven people is a lean, not a call.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Not holding up' with '0 of 7 at $599 or more, once · then: 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month · bar 5 of 7 on each' right beside it, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b3: It is my Price line, but writing it as '$599 up front, then $20 a month' makes Pro sound mandatory, when my ladder is $599 with free unlimited captions up to $839 a year with Pro, so the monthly count tests a tier I never required.
screens.why_b4: Beyond the 'When a line fails' header there is no line on what to do. It never says that most would pay $250 to $599, or that the 'try a demo first' answers point at my existing 15-day free returns, which they clearly did not know about.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible ('7 against · 6 asked their why here · 1 never saw it (Amaka)'), every quote carries its price bands, and nothing claims beyond the six who answered.
screens.why_b6: I did not type that people want to trial it in their own hard moment (a matinee under stage lights, a noisy walk), that its worth hinges on catching audience questions and eleven overlapping voices rather than one speaker, or that one-sided deafness has a cheap seat-choice workaround. Each of these adds to what I wrote.
screens.instead: Price failed at $599, but 5 of 6 put it at $250 to under $599: try a lower entry price or lead with the 15-day free returns, since two asked for a trial pair, and prove multi-speaker pickup, which two named as what would make it worth more.

screens.why1: As the first screen it's an obvious check that I'm someone who mixes with hearing people, before anything else is asked.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is how we say it in my world, and I can answer straight away; my only small doubt is whether 'talk' counts texting or the chat at work, but I'd still say yes without a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly how often I'm face to face with hearing people: at the shop, at work, with family.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it for a weekly-or-not screener, and no escape is right on a gate question.
screens.why5: It's the founder's 'talk with hearing people every week' word for word, and nothing about any product or app leaks through.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and 'Yes or no' is easy to take in in one go, though as a deaf person I'd be reading the captions rather than hearing it.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes; No

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to show me the idea before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: Live captions and keeping eye contact are exactly the words I use; 'The people nearby talk' is a little stiff but I get it on first read.
screens.why3: Losing the conversation because I'm looking down at my phone's captions instead of at the person is my week, so I can picture this straight away.
screens.why4: It is a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It tells me plainly what the glasses do and who believes what, with no company jargon or labels for people like me.
screens.why6: Short plain sentences with no slashes, brackets or numbers, so I could follow it heard once, as long as I can see the speaker or a transcript.

screens.why1: After asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask how often those conversations get away from me.
screens.why2: 'Miss' could mean I wasn't there at all or that I sat through it and lost the thread, and for me it's usually the second, so I'd have to stop and decide which one you mean.
screens.why3: I lose parts of most conversations at work, at the shops or round a noisy table, so putting one number on a whole month means I'd be guessing.
screens.why4: A number box with 'None' and 'I can't recall' works, but 'I'd rather not say' is a second escape the screen shouldn't have.
screens.why5: The founder's window is the last seven days and the situation is a conversation too fast or noisy to follow, but this asks about last month and about 'missed' conversations, which drifts from both.
screens.why6: The question itself says fine, but 'a number of conversations last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a mouthful, and 'none is 0' sounds odd when heard.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, how many conversations with hearing people were too fast or noisy for you to follow? A number; or say I can't recall.

screens.why1: Asking what the glasses are worth makes sense after the idea card, but it comes right after one question about missed conversations, and the kicker still says 'What you do today' when this is about the idea, not my day.
screens.why2: 'Up front' and 'a month' are how I'd talk about buying hearing aids and a captioning app, so I get it on first reading.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids and caption apps, so I know roughly what something like this is worth to me, even though I haven't seen these glasses.
screens.why4: The bands cover everything and don't overlap, but the $599 edge looks like a price someone already set, odd next to the round $250 and $1,000.
screens.why5: The $599 edge reads like the company's own sticker price showing through, which drifts from asking what it's worth to me.
screens.why6: Four options, then two, is easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' is clumsy to hear, and I'd hear two prices, one-off and monthly, back to back.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? Under $500; $500 to under $1,000; $1,000 to under $2,500; $2,500 or more; or I wouldn't pay for this. Escape: I can't say.

screens.why1: It comes straight after I put a price on AirCaps, so asking what would make it worth more is the obvious next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: Every word is plain to me, and I can answer it on first reading, for example 'if it kept up in a noisy restaurant' or 'if it showed who is talking'.
screens.why3: I can answer from my own life, from the dinners and meetings where I lose the thread, and I don't need to know anything about how the company works.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: AirCaps was shown to me on purpose on the idea card, and nothing else from the founder's plan or their words for people comes through.
screens.why6: It is one short question that I can hold, but 'two hundred fifty to under five hundred ninety-nine dollars' is a mouthful to hear read back, and the odd 599 doesn't say well.
screens.instead: You gave AirCaps a price a moment ago. What would it have to do for you to pay more?

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on AirCaps, asking whether anyone else had a say the last time I bought something like it makes sense, though the kicker jumps from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5.
screens.why2: 'Something like this' makes me stop and think whether it means my hearing aids, a captioning app or the glasses, and the question only asks who agreed when what matters for me is often who paid.
screens.why3: I have bought hearing aids and apps, but insurance, Vocational Rehab or my employer often had a say or paid, and none of the options lets me say that, so I would be guessing.
screens.why4: 'No, someone else decided for me' sits oddly under 'No' because it really means my say wasn't needed, the yes and no options alternate instead of grouping, there is no option for insurance or an agency paying, and 'I can't recall one' doesn't fit a question that never asked me to recall 'one'.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product or roles leaks here; it is a plain question about whether anyone else had to agree when I paid.
screens.why6: Four options heard as yes, no, yes, no are hard to hold and easy to mix up, and 'or say you can't recall one' leaves me asking 'one what?'.
screens.instead: The last time you paid for a hearing device or captioning tool, who decided? I decided alone · Someone else had to agree · Someone else decided for me · Insurance or an agency decided — or: I can't recall

screens.why1: After I've put a price on AirCaps and said who has to agree, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the natural last question, though the kicker 'What you do today' doesn't fit it.
screens.why2: Order a pair, free returns, ready today: I'd understand all of it on the first hearing.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd send for glasses that caption the people talking to me if I could send them back, so I'm answering for myself, not guessing.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided: there's a 'Probably not' but no 'Probably yes', so someone leaning yes who wants to see the accuracy first has to jump to a full yes or a no.
screens.why5: 'Live captions inside your glasses' is plain, says what the thing is, and nothing of anyone's business plan or roles comes through.
screens.why6: One short question and three short options I can hold after hearing them once, with no escape owed on a commitment question.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order a pair with free returns, or not? — Yes, I'd order a pair · Probably yes · Probably not · No
